cs.signsync.title: SignSync
cs.signsync.subtitle: Learning sign language through visual digital nudges and spatial computing.
cs.signsync.body_0: At the Apple Developer Academy, a conversation with a deaf teacher changed my perspective. We had to use an interpreter, and she told me something that stuck: in many situations, her smartphone is her 'best friend.' It made me realize that communication isn't a given.
cs.signsync.body_1: I also learned that not all deaf people know sign language, often because traditional courses are inaccessible. That gap felt like something technology could actually bridge.
cs.signsync.body_2: Sign language is motor learning. Small variations in hand position can completely change a gesture's meaning. Yet, most learning tools rely on videos. You watch a screen, try to mimic it, and guess if you got it right.
cs.signsync.body_3: The challenge was: how do you teach a precise physical skill without trapping the user behind a 2D screen or interrupting them with constant corrections?
cs.signsync.body_4: My master's thesis explored how visual digital nudges influence decisions. SignSync tests if those same principles can guide motor learning.
cs.signsync.body_5: Instead of explicit instructions, the experience uses semi-transparent 'ghost hands' in spatial computing. They act as visual nudges—guiding attention and encouraging imitation in real-time, right next to the user's own hands.
cs.signsync.body_6: Designed for Apple Vision Pro, SignSync shifts learning from translation (watching a screen and copying) to direct spatial imitation. While currently a research concept focused on sign language, the broader question it asks is whether spatial nudges can transform how we acquire any physical skill—from rehabilitation to education.
cs.deal.title: Deal!
cs.deal.subtitle: Solving the Abilene Paradox through private decisions.
cs.deal.body_0: "I'm fine with whatever." "If everyone else is down..." "Next time, someone else chooses!"
cs.deal.body_1: We've all heard these sentences. It's called the Abilene Paradox: a situation where a group agrees on a plan that nobody actually wanted, just to avoid conflict. During the project, my team and I realized we weren't just designing for a target audience—we were the target audience.
cs.deal.body_2: If someone suggests grabbing a beer, you might say yes just because you think everyone else wants to. Before you know it, the whole group has agreed on something nobody genuinely wanted to do.
cs.deal.body_3: The challenge was: how do we design an experience where friends can express what they actually want to do, without social pressure swaying their answers?
cs.deal.body_4: We solved this by making preferences invisible. Users create activity cards for things they'd genuinely like to do. Friends then privately swipe on these ideas.
cs.deal.body_5: The swipe interaction was deliberately chosen to encourage instinctive, honest responses rather than overthinking. A plan only surfaces when there's a match. Because we were handling delicate social dynamics, privacy was paramount—we integrated Sign in with Apple to hide emails and keep interactions completely confidential by default.
cs.deal.body_6: Developed within a multidisciplinary team of six, my contribution focused on UX design, user flows, and navigation patterns following Apple's Human Interface Guidelines.
cs.deal.body_7: One of the main design challenges was structuring an intuitive app flow without relying on a traditional tab bar.
cs.poly.title: PolyEscape
cs.poly.subtitle: A puzzle experience shaped through iterative player testing.
cs.poly.body_0: Many puzzle games fall into two extremes: too simplistic and shallow, or overly complex with a high cognitive load. PolyEscape was built in Unity with Borum Studio to find the sweet spot: a puzzle-exploration game that is easy to learn, but deeply engaging.
cs.poly.body_1: Our first prototype featured a strict UI color system to reduce cognitive load. But testing revealed a deeper problem: mechanical clarity wasn't enough. Players felt lost on every level. They didn't know what to do, where to go, or why it mattered.
cs.poly.body_2: Each round of testing translated a single insight into a concrete design decision. Four iterations reshaped how the game communicates without explaining.
cs.poly.point_desc_0: Light narrative cues replace static instructions.
cs.poly.point_desc_1: The city itself signals direction and progress.
cs.poly.point_desc_2: Pacing adjusts to keep tension calibrated.
cs.poly.point_desc_3: A throughline gives every level a reason to matter.
cs.poly.body_3: Developed alongside designers and developers at Borum Studio, my contribution went beyond early UX/UI design to include game mechanics and Player Experience (PX) testing. The core focus was translating user friction into targeted environmental design solutions.
cs.poly.body_4: Environmental storytelling and recognizable landmarks naturally guide players through the world.
cs.poly.body_5: PolyEscape successfully shipped to the App Store.
cs.foto.title: Il Progetto Fotovoltaico
cs.foto.subtitle: Building a visual identity for a sub-brand in the renewable energy sector.
cs.foto.body_0: The client offered a solid service but lacked a clear identity. The brief was to convey a sense of familiarity while leveraging the existing presence of La Casa del Fotovoltaico, as Il Progetto Fotovoltaico was conceived as its sub-brand.
cs.foto.body_1: How can a new brand establish its own personality while maintaining continuity with an already recognizable parent brand?
cs.foto.body_2: Color carries meaning before words do. The palette evokes sunlight without falling into environmentalist clichés — warm, clean tones that read as professional and approachable. A modern sans-serif completes the system, legible at any size.
cs.foto.body_3: My contribution focused on brand identity and visual design, helping define a coherent visual language capable of balancing familiarity and differentiation.
cs.foto.label_4: A system, not just a logo
cs.foto.body_4: A consistent identity system was developed to create a recognizable sub-brand while preserving the trust and credibility associated with the parent company. Typography, colours, and graphic elements were designed to strengthen the relationship between the two brands without sacrificing the individuality of the new venture.
cs.unblinking.title: Unblinking
cs.unblinking.subtitle: An interactive experience about judgment and identity.
cs.unblinking.body_0: Many people learn to hide parts of themselves in order to be accepted. Unblinking translates this emotional condition into an interactive experience.
cs.unblinking.body_1: A flame represents anyone who has ever felt exposed under the gaze of others. As pressure increases, the flame weakens and hides behind a mask — a visual language for concealment that needs no explanation.
cs.unblinking.body_2: How can an interactive experience encourage reflection without imposing a single interpretation?
cs.unblinking.body_3: Animations only carry meaning if everyone can perceive them. Accessibility was treated as a design constraint from the start, not an afterthought.
cs.unblinking.point_desc_0: High-contrast states at every stage of the animation.
cs.unblinking.point_desc_1: Narration adapts to the state of the experience.
cs.unblinking.point_desc_2: Every element labeled for assistive technology.
cs.unblinking.point_desc_4: Visuals respond directly to user interaction.
cs.unblinking.body_4: I was responsible for UX design, asset creation, interaction design, and SwiftUI development.
cs.unblinking.body_5: A flame acts as a metaphor for identity, transforming emotional states into interactive experiences.
cs.unblinking.label_6: Developed for the Apple Swift Student Challenge, Unblinking explores how interactive experiences can foster self-awareness.
cs.snapyap.title: SnapYap
cs.snapyap.subtitle: Transforming photographs into multisensory memories.
cs.snapyap.body_0: We initially set out to build a color-to-sound app. But a few days in, our team realized the idea lacked emotional longevity—it was a gimmick, not a product. We scrapped it and pivoted to a much simpler mission: creating something that actually replicates how human memory works.
cs.snapyap.label_1: Why not just record a video?
cs.snapyap.body_1: Human memory doesn't work like a video recorder; it stores frozen mental images anchored to specific sounds and feelings. Video recordings, on the other hand, often feel performative and cause sensory overload. The challenge was: how do we design a digital memory that feels as authentic and spontaneous as a real one?
cs.snapyap.body_2: SnapYAP transforms standard photographs into multisensory memories by blending static images with personal voice notes.
cs.snapyap.body_3: To save a photo, the user is required to speak. This isn't just a technical requirement—it's a conscious ritual. It forces you to stop and process the moment. By keeping the visual static and letting the audio become the narrator, SnapYAP acts as a private digital diary rather than a performance.
cs.snapyap.body_4: Working alongside a team of designers and developers, my role focused on UX/UI design. My main focus was shaping the core interaction flow—specifically the mechanic that ties the act of speaking directly to the image development process.
cs.tesi.title: Nudge & Neuromarketing
cs.tesi.subtitle: Exploring how behavioural design influences sustainable decisions.
cs.tesi.body_0: This research project investigates how subtle interface changes can encourage users to make more sustainable choices.
cs.tesi.body_1: Can digital nudges influence environmentally conscious decisions without restricting freedom of choice?
cs.tesi.body_2: Two versions of an e-commerce checkout (MarketPlace.it) were built in Figma. The control version presented delivery options neutrally. The experimental version introduced a visual nudge — icons, colors and microcopy implying environmental impact, without ever naming "sustainability".
cs.tesi.point_desc_1: Color and iconography imply environmental impact.
cs.tesi.body_3: My contribution focused on UX research and interaction design.
cs.tesi.body_4: Different interface solutions were explored to understand how visual digital nudges affect user behaviour.
cs.tesi.stat_label_2: Did not consciously notice the nudge
cs.tvtime.title: TV Time
cs.tvtime.subtitle: Redesigning a familiar experience through Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines.
cs.tvtime.label_0: Designing what I use every day
cs.tvtime.body_0: I've used TV Time almost every day for years. When you use an app that much, you don't just see its features—you feel its friction. Despite a great community, the interface felt cluttered, and worst of all, it felt sluggish. I decided to sit down and redesign the tool I open every night.
cs.tvtime.body_1: How do you fix an app that feels slow without touching the backend code? The challenge was improving the perceived performance and cleaning up the information architecture, without alienating millions of users who already rely on the current layout.
cs.tvtime.body_2: I stripped back the visual noise and rebuilt the core flows strictly following Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (HIG). By leveraging native design patterns, standard typography scales, and familiar navigation structures, the interface not only looked cleaner—it felt immediately faster and more responsive.
cs.tvtime.body_3: Beyond the visual cleanup, I designed a brand-new spoiler-protection system. Using a native-feeling toggle and a dynamic blurring system, the feature allows users to safely browse discussions and rate episodes without the constant anxiety of a ruined plot twist.
cs.tvtime.body_4: As a solo passion project, I handled the entire process: auditing the existing UX, restructuring the information architecture, and designing the new UI to strict HIG standards.
cs.eclissi.title: ECLISSI
cs.eclissi.subtitle: Creating a visual identity inspired by mystery and elegance.
cs.eclissi.body_0: ECLISSI is a premium event space designed as an elegant, safe alternative to traditional nightclubs. Targeting a 25-40 demographic, the business goal was clear: move away from one-off events and build a loyal community around a high-end, reassuring nightlife experience.
cs.eclissi.body_1: How do you visually communicate 'premium' without feeling elitist? The challenge was balancing mystery with accessibility. The visual identity needed to signal a sophisticated, secure environment, especially for a female audience, while avoiding the clichés of typical club branding.
cs.eclissi.body_2: The palette starts from a deep, almost midnight black, with cold gold as the only accent — not warm color, but color that signals who belongs. A modern serif carries the headlines; a compact sans handles the body copy.
cs.eclissi.body_3: I led the brand strategy and visual execution—translating the business goal of a safe, premium nightlife experience into a comprehensive visual identity, logo design, and social media direction.
cs.eclissi.body_4: A complete brand guideline and digital presence. The visual language establishes ECLISSI not just as a location, but as a modern, sophisticated destination with a clear standard of quality.
cs.pollino.title: Pollino Flower Park
cs.pollino.subtitle: Building visibility for a hidden gem.
cs.pollino.body_0: Pollino Flower Park initially had no online presence. The goal was to transform it into a recognizable destination for eco-tourists and outdoor enthusiasts.
cs.pollino.body_1: How can visual storytelling communicate the values of eco-hospitality and slow tourism?
cs.pollino.body_2: The visual system and content plan were built around the location's strongest asset: the experience itself.
cs.pollino.point_desc_0: Imagery built around the natural setting.
cs.pollino.point_desc_1: Content centered on what guests actually do.
cs.pollino.point_desc_2: One voice across every channel and touchpoint.
cs.pollino.body_3: My work focused on visual storytelling, social media strategy, and content creation.
cs.pollino.body_4: Nature and outdoor experiences became the core elements of the brand identity.
cs.pollino.label_5: The project generated significant growth in visibility and audience engagement.
